item.title: The Suicides We're Not Counting
item.description:
Suicide

The Suicides We're Not Counting

America's suicide rate is rising. The real number of suicides may be much higher than the official one.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • U.S. suicide rose 37.5% from 2000 to 2024, but drug-poisoning deaths rose 3.5-fold.
  • Many overdose deaths that are truly suicides are recorded as "accidents" — perhaps up to 30%.
  • A behavior-based measure and a death-certificate checkbox could reveal the hidden toll.

When someone dies of a drug overdose, a medical examiner or coroner faces a judgment call that shapes both a family’s grief and a nation’s statistics: Was it an accident, or did the person mean to die? It sounds like a question with a clear answer. In practice, it is among the hardest determinations in all of medicine and public health — and I have come to believe we are getting it wrong more often than we used to.

I have spent much of my career as an injury epidemiologist studying how we count deaths, and I’ve reached an unsettling conclusion: American suicide accounting has deteriorated over the past 25 years, even as suicide itself has climbed.

Consider the numbers. Between 2000 and 2024, the national suicide rate rose 37.5%. Over the same stretch, the drug-poisoning death rate rose three and a half times. Yet the rate of deaths officially recorded as drug-poisoning suicides barely moved — drifting between 1.3 and 1.8 per 100,000 people, even as pills and fentanyl grew far more lethal and far more available. That gap should give us pause. By our best estimate, up to 30% of overdose deaths may in fact be suicides that were never recorded as such.

The problem is part human, part structural. Suicide has always been stigmatized — shadowed by religious condemnation, legal prohibition, and insurance clauses that punish grieving families. Relatives may resist the label; investigators, sensitive to that pain and short on time, may reach for a gentler one. And the people who make these calls — medical examiners and coroners — have been overwhelmed, first by the opioid epidemic and then by COVID-19, which buried them under what one colleague described as the “piling of bodies.”

To classify a death as suicide, an investigator generally needs evidence of intent: a note, a psychiatric history, a record of prior attempts — some sign the person wanted to die. A gunshot wound or a hanging is forensically overt. A drug overdose is quiet and ambiguous. When corroborating evidence is missing, as it so often is, the default becomes “accident.”

We cannot prevent what we cannot see. And the deaths we miss are not missed at random.

We have known how to do better for a long time. In mid-20th-century Los Angeles County, a wave of barbiturate deaths defied easy classification. A team from the Los Angeles Suicide Prevention Center — the psychologists Edwin Shneidman and Norman Farberow, the psychiatrist Robert Litman, and the chief county coroner, Theodore (Ted) Curphey — pioneered what Shneidman called the “psychological autopsy”: a careful reconstruction of a person’s final weeks through records and interviews with those who knew them. It worked, uncovering hidden suicidality in cases that had looked equivocal. Then, largely because of cost and inertia, the practice faded. That cost looks trivial beside a recent estimate that suicide drains American society of roughly half a trillion dollars a year.

Why does the miscounting matter so much? Because the deaths we overlook are not missed at random. The undercounting falls more heavily on some groups than others. Using a broader, behavior-based measure my colleagues and I call self-injury mortality, we found that from 2008 to 2017 such deaths rose 109% among Black Americans, against 55% among white Americans — and faster among women than men. Official suicide statistics hide those divergences. If we can’t see who is dying, we can’t design prevention that reaches them.

So, what would help? A shift in how we think about these deaths. Rather than staking everything on inferring what a person intended in their final moments — often unknowable — we can pay attention to how they lived in the weeks before: the patterned, repetitive self-harm of escalating substance use. Self-injury mortality gathers registered suicides together with the great majority of overdose deaths that reflect that behavior, whatever we can affirm about intent. A concrete first step would be adding a self-injury checkbox to the U.S. death certificate — one that cuts across suicide, “accident,” and undetermined — so this hidden toll finally becomes visible to the people who plan prevention and treatment.

The stakes are only rising. With economic turbulence, cuts to the social safety net, and the early signs of an opioid crisis reaching Europe, this is no moment to look away from the deaths we aren’t counting. The first task of prevention is honest arithmetic. We owe the people we’ve lost — and the ones we still might save — an accurate count.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: How Moments of Awe Unlock Creative Thinking
item.description:
Awe

How Moments of Awe Unlock Creative Thinking

Awe makes creativity happen in multiple ways.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Awe has been proven to stimulate creative endeavors.
  • Awe is not just about big events, but lots of small ones, too.
  • When we include awe as an everyday experience, our creative spirit soars.

The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley, defines awe as “that goose-bumpy sensation that we get in the presence of something profound: something greater, more powerful, or more eternal than ourselves. It arises when we encounter things that challenge our sense of what’s normal or possible.”

In my research for a recent book, I had the opportunity to touch the bark of a tree more than 5,000 years old, to kayak through a congress of resplendent bald cypresses, to watch a magnificent dance of leaves in an old-growth forest, and to observe a blood-red sunrise over a grove of aspens. Each was awesome; each was an experience that engaged my senses, stimulated my creative instincts, and propelled my fingers across a computer keyboard faster than I thought possible. My imagination was truly energized! Let’s examine that connection.

What the Research on Awe Says

A research review reveals several studies that have either examined the relationship between awe and creativity or identified mechanisms (such as curiosity and cognitive flexibility) that underscore this unique relationship. Here are three examples:

In the most recent study (2026), researchers conducted complementary studies using surveys, experimental awe videos, and creativity assessments. What they discovered was that individuals demonstrated significantly higher levels of creativity after an “awesome” event. So, too, did awe increase their cognitive flexibility as well as creative self-efficacy. The researchers noted that these two variables helped participants form sequential pathways that explained why an awesome event boosts individual creativity.

An earlier study (2023) looked at 257 adults to examine creative changes over a four-month period. The researchers discovered that awe doesn’t just make people feel inspired; it changes the way they think by increasing mental flexibility and confidence in generating novel ideas. One of the key takeaways was that awe seems to cultivate creativity indirectly by stimulating curiosity—a motivational engine underlying creative exploration.

Subsequently, a 2025 study examined how awe enhances the mental conditions that support creative thinking. Participants assigned to an awe-intervention group reported greater awe, lower stress, and improved psychological well-being when compared to those in a control group. The researchers concluded that reduced stress and greater cognitive openness create conditions that facilitate creative insight and flexible problem-solving.

Research Overview

Additional research supports the interconnections between experiences of awe and improved creative thinking. These include the following:

1. Awe has a tendency to expand our mental horizons, moving beyond familiar patterns while creating new ones.

2. Awe increases our openness to new experiences; as such, we ask more questions and explore more possibilities.

3. Awe stimulates and encourages curiosity; it helps us look at things with new eyes.

4. Awe promotes cognitive flexibility; we begin to see multiple possibilities rather than single answers. So too, do we generate novel associations and connect seemingly unrelated ideas.

Source: dopefreak_creations/Pixabay

Putting Research Into Practice

It is clear that awe broadens our attention, increases cognitive flexibility, and stimulates our inherent curiosity—all necessary for creativity to happen. To that end, here are a few activities for your consideration:

1. Awe Walk: Leave your phone at home and walk through your neighborhood for 30 minutes. Look up (instead of down), intentionally noticing things often taken for granted: the unique shape of a cloud, the singular pattern of a tree’s bark, the dulcet song of a bird, the commanding architecture of a building, or a splash of light upon a car window. Keep asking yourself, “What have I never noticed before?”

2. Expand Your Reading: Regularly select some nonfiction reading material about a topic you know little about. This may include topics such as Irish lighthouses, Egyptian archeology, the physics of water, how trees communicate, or nocturnal mammals (for example). Keep asking, “What can I learn here that I didn’t know previously?” Marvel at the discoveries.

3. Awe Journal: Maintain a notebook into which you record awesome events. Try to pen an experience regularly—one that makes you say “Wow!” or “Amazing!” These may include a beautiful piece of music, a rediscovered photograph, someone’s unexpected question, the playfulness of a child, or an unusual gift. For each entry, record how the event expanded your thinking.

4. For the First Time: Each day, select a common object and pretend you are seeing it for the first time. For example: a fallen leaf, a spoon, your fingers, a button, a weed in your garden, or a neighbor’s house. Ask yourself, “What is something new here that I haven’t noticed before?” Seeing the familiar differently will supercharge your creativity.

5. Celebration Awe: Some of the most delightful examples of awe are when we recognize the kindness, outreach, and generosity of others. The best question we can ask ourselves is, “Who inspired me today?” The response might be a teenager assisting an elderly person with her groceries, a police officer rescuing a brood of baby ducks from a storm drain, or a neighbor facing a medical hardship with uncommon courage.

6. Unanswered Questions: Get in the habit of asking and recording questions with no easy answers. A few examples may include, “Why are some birds flightless?”, “Why do children invent imaginary friends?”, “How did early fish (Tiktaalik) crawl up on land?”, or “How do we know the universe is expanding?” Don’t answer the questions, just continue to collect them. This regularly stimulates your curiosity while expanding your cognitive flexibility.

7. Travel Awe: Make it a regular practice to experience something that truly amazes and delights—both near and far. For example, examine a geological wonder (e.g., Arches National Park), journey to a local cathedral, roam a botanical garden, visit a planetarium, or discover an urban art museum. These are opportunities for your mind to experience “newness” and celebrate a vast array of original discoveries.

Devotion to the incorporation of awesome activities into your daily life will widen your attention, quiet your inner critic, and remind you that there is a marvelous array of new discoveries that supersede everyday routines. And in that noticing, you will begin to create. Guaranteed.

item.title: Does Your College Student Have ADHD?
item.description:
ADHD

Does Your College Student Have ADHD?

13 ways to best support your child in preparation for college.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • College offers new opportunities and challenges for students with ADHD.
  • Parents can help by making sure their child is aware of key campus resources and organizational tools.
  • Knowing in advance where to find a good doctor and get medication if they need it is also valuable.

The majority of parents of college-bound students are understandably concerned about what the transition will be like for both their children and themselves. Perhaps you’re a parent reading this, and you have high hopes for your child to go off to college and have a successful journey, both academically and socially. But if you’re a parent of a child with ADHD, you may have other concerns and worries. This article addresses how to deal with those.

Source: Brooke Cagle/ Unsplash

As a college professor for over 30 years, I have witnessed the proliferation of this diagnosis among my students. Sometimes it is a formal diagnosis by a physician, and other times students have self-diagnosed, knowing that they have some learning differences. In my new book, I address over a hundred issues to help the full range of students, and here I will specifically focus on how to best support your student with ADHD.

1. Understand what the college experience actually is.

It’s important to remember and to convey to your child that above all, college is a process for figuring out how to learn, how to think, and how to manage life. That means that this is an ongoing process that can’t be fully figured out and determined before college as much as we might want to do that.

Parents are often hoping for quick fixes, especially for the summer between high school graduation and the beginning of college. And while it’s a good time to do certain preparatory things to feel ready, it’s the experience of being in college that will help students figure out some of the things that work best for them.

2. Procrastination is common in college, and it’s certainly very common among students with ADHD.

However, research shows that procrastination is often because of a fear of failure as well as a fear of success, yet the good news is that procrastination generally lessens as we get older.

3. The single, most important thing that students can do is to invest in a calendar system that can work for and with them.

And by invest, I really mean psychologically. There are plenty of online tools for this, though experience tells me that the act of writing it down is essential. Just as research shows that taking handwritten notes during a lecture is most effective, it is also the case that paper calendars and lists can ensure that nothing is out of sight and out of mind.

The act of writing something down can make it more indelible in our memory. People with ADHD often function better when they can see something and be reminded of it.

4. It’s really important to go through each syllabus thoroughly.

See what each professor is expecting in the class, and enter due dates into a calendar as well as dates by which certain projects need to be started. This can be done in a fun way with colored markers to signify different courses.

5. Students often benefit from also making a master list of everything that they need to do with due dates (soonest to farthest out), so that they can see this in both list and calendar form.

Project management works best when things are broken up into smaller, manageable chunks with goals and dates.

6. Students with ADHD benefit from having classes scheduled every day or almost every day.

This means there is a constant touchstone, and there aren’t fully open days with seemingly aimless time. For most people, knowing that they have the entire day can feel both wonderful and freeing but also overwhelming once in it. Students might find that they actually get more done in the hour or two between things than they do when they have five wide-open hours in front of them.

7. Know your campus resources.

Students can benefit from campus centers that provide more information, tools, and resources for dealing with these issues, as well as ways to connect with others who have dealt with these issues. This includes offices like the academic success center, tutoring center, and counseling center, many of which host workshops on time management, stress reduction, study habits, effective reading, etc.

8. Students benefit from a well-designed schedule, but one that also has some room for the spontaneity that helps them be who they are.

Things like regular exercise, nutritious meals, time in nature, reduced screen time, and good sleep support all of this.

9. It’s important to help support students in ways that don’t let the diagnosis define them.

In recent years, students have become so open about mental health issues that they are also talking about this in a way that enables them to take it on as their main identity.

10. The reality is that we live in a society that has an oversaturation of information and so many different things pulling on our attention and energy.

All of that generates a lot of outside noise and internal noise. Grounding practices that help to center the body and mind can be useful for people with ADHD or for anyone really, including yoga and meditation.

11. Students are often well served by being open with their professors about any issues they have.

There are many professors who themselves struggle with ADHD, anxiety, depression, etc., and they may even feel comfortable sharing what does and doesn’t work for them.

12. Have an open conversation about the extent to which your student plans to make use of the Office for Students with Disabilities.

Be sure to have all documentation that will be required if accommodations are going to be utilized. Consider role-playing situations for how best to self-advocate.

13. If your student is treated with medication, be sure to locate a psychiatrist, therapist, and pharmacy near campus.

item.title: A Celebration of Our Close Kinship with Other Primates
item.description:
Environment

A Celebration of Our Close Kinship with Other Primates

Lennette Newell's new book is a science-based photographic gem.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • The first of its kind, it offers rare all-access insights into these uniquely mesmerizing animals.
  • The intrigue of observing each species brings deep understanding of commonalities that lead to coexistence.
  • The book seeks to inspire empathy and responsibility for primates through visual storytelling.
Critically endangered Western lowland gorilla.
Source: Lennette Newell

While there are a good number of photographic books about a wide variety of non-human primates, renowned photographer Lennette Newell's new book Primates: A Kinship with All Creatures stands out by offering unique, science-based insights into this group of fascinating, diverse mammals. Here's what she had to say about this highly unique collection of photographs and facts.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you publish Primates: A Kinship with All Creatures?

Lennette Newell: I did not set out to do a primate book. I started photographing some primates that were confiscated after being brought into the U.S. on the black market. My work as a commercial photographer (in the niche market of pet advertising) gave me contacts across the entire animal network. I was able to photograph these primates, and from there my interest only grew. I began photographing every available situation, whether in a studio set at a facility or at a location; it became a fascination I wanted to share with a broader audience. My world has become clearer through these experiences, and they have brought to light just how important each and every species is to our own survival.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

LN: My life started on a ranch in the high plains where my father was a large-animal veterinarian. I was surrounded by animals from birth; they were part of our larger family. The animals were my teachers, my companions, providing knowledge and comfort, and I zigged and zagged with their body language completely; their flow of emotions entertained me, saddened me, and became my world. All animals share a common language, while each species has its own hierarchy. Our commonalities are truly the same. We all show affection and love, grieve, express stress, and, if necessary, threaten in order to save ourselves and our family. I have always loved all creatures, and my curiosity only grows with age for a glimpse into other creatures’ souls less known to me. The intrigue of observing each species brings more questions and a deeper understanding that our commonalities lead to healthy coexistence.

Source: G Editions/with permission.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

LN: Everyone, young kids who look at photos, curious humans, animal lovers, suspicious folks who are unsure why I call them our relatives, nature and sustainability advocates, corporate executives, and all primate specialists, psychologists, and passionate souls whose love for all creatures will help save them. Kinship is nature.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

LN: I am a compassionate photographer, presenting images of these primates who came before us millions of years ago as creatures equal to us and valued as any Homo sapiens would be. There is no question I am connected to them and find inspiration in each species, expanding my own knowledge of myself.

The images presented in the book are black-and-white; it is a love story to my viewers. Hold the portraits close to your heart with no distractions. Examine the whole of every image and its details; close the book after a session and come back to admire and ponder what you believe transpired in this moment. Consider our kinship. Contemplate our responsibility to those creatures who have come before us. Celebrate the natural world we live in.

All primates live in fragile ecosystems with many under pressure from climate change, habitat loss, and an imbalance due to disease and other factors. Primates had a larger territory to live in decades ago, which allowed younger primates to breed with other troops, keeping their DNA strong. Now the neighboring troop, which also lives close to their troop, is the only choice due to habitat loss. As their territory becomes smaller, many elements of their ecosystem are disappearing, degrading the quality of life for many primate species.

Endangered proboscis monkey.
Source: Lennette Newell.

Every habitat, whether natural or in an accredited sanctuary, zoo, or conservation center, is important for the survival of primate species. If you live in California, you can visit the Gibbon Conservation Center where I photographed the gibbons for the book. You can also explore the New England Primate Conservancy for more detailed knowledge about these animals.

Animals should not be viewed as products but as part of our valued natural world. Some primates are understandably hunted for food. Our view of the natural world needs to change. How does this happen? I share my most compassionate visuals in hopes people will connect; on a larger scale, organizations such as the world-renowned Jane Goodall Institute are at the forefront of showing why we need to work for peaceful coexistence rather than exploitation.

My journey to Borneo included the Borneo Nature Lodge. They work closely with Tomoko Kanamori of Japan’s Orangutan Research Center. They have a first-generation forest, one of the few remaining; it is incredibly beautiful. The guides were able to spot the orangutans due to the researchers on the ground. This cohesive arrangement ensures revenue to the government from tourists, protects the primates, and supports Japan’s Orangutan Research Center’s work.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

LN: I approached this as a photographer; therefore, my book is a visual story with intimate, personal black-and-white photographs. The time I spent with each primate was one of respect and shared interconnection. Our understanding of each other was naturally instinctive for both of us. I use the word instinctive quite a bit. I feel my movements, my thoughts, the thoughts of the primates, and their movements become one, as if we have known each other for a while; nothing to think about; our language coincides. This natural cohesion brings forth the photographs I present in this book for further evaluation, open to each viewer’s wonder and creativity.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about these amazing beings they will treat them with more respect, compassion, and dignity?

LN: Yes, to quote Jane Goodall, “Only if we understand will we care.”

This book required years of photography, and I loved each minute. This understanding and these experiences deepened my respect for Mother Nature. Simply magnificent, to this day I am overwhelmed with this gift that only requires respect and careful thought to live within this abundance, carefully using our sense of selves that weaves a natural web to our shared ecosystems.

item.title: The Difference Between Needs and Wants
item.description:
Parenting

The Difference Between Needs and Wants

What parents call needs are usually strategies, and naming the real need helps.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • A need is what you require to thrive. A want is the specific form you're hoping that need arrives in.
  • Most parent frustrations — from messy houses to partner conflicts — point to needs for ease, rest, or support.
  • When both people's needs are visible, conflicts stop being about who wins and start being about what works.

I remember saying to my daughter when she was about two: "You WANT to play, but I NEED to cook dinner."

It felt true in the moment. The cooking was urgent and playing was optional — something that could happen once the chores were done. One was a need, one was a want, and I got to decide which was which.

Then I learned that the way I was thinking about it was making things harder.

What Are Needs?

In Nonviolent Communication (NVC), needs are what every person — adult or child — requires to feel grounded, connected, and at ease. And what we tend to call our "needs" as parents — getting dinner cooked, having the house under control, getting everyone out the door — are often wants, or strategies: one specific way we're hoping a real need will get met.

Meanwhile, what we tend to dismiss as our children's "wants" — play, physical closeness, having a say, being taken seriously — are needs too.

In NVC, a need is something people require in order to thrive, including physical needs like food and water, and intangible ones like respect, meaning, and connection.

The needs list organizes these into eight categories:

  • Connection: acceptance, belonging, love, empathy, trust, being understood
  • Peace: calm, ease, order, harmony, respect
  • Honesty: authenticity, integrity, presence
  • Meaning: growth, creativity, learning, purpose, competence
  • Safety: consistency, physical and emotional security
  • Autonomy: choice, freedom, independence, space
  • Relaxation/Leisure: play, fun, rest, joy, mental space
  • Physical Well-Being: food, water, sleep, exercise, self-care

Note that this list is not exhaustive — it’s intended to be an approachable starting point for overwhelmed parents.

Evidence indicates that needs of autonomy, competence, and connectedness are somewhat universal, although individuals have variations in how strongly they show up.

Kids with strong sensory needs might not be able to do anything before their need for comfort is met. Many autistic kids feel much more settled when their needs for order and consistency are met. Most parents I work with have strong needs for rest, ease, and collaboration. ‘

Different people, different needs — but we all have them in some form.

What Is the Difference Between Needs and Wants?

A want isn't the opposite of a need. A want is one specific way you picture a need getting met.

The need might be rest, mental space, or ease. The want is the particular form you're hoping that need arrives in. "I need you to stop jumping on the couch" is one strategy to meet a need for mental space. But it's not the only one. I could move to another room. I could put on headphones. I could look at what my child needs — movement, attention — and address that instead.

One parent described it to me this way: "The idea that I could change my behavior to meet my need was revelatory."

When you're locked onto one specific strategy, you and the other person are working against each other. When you can name the underlying need, more paths open up.

What Parents Call "Needs" Are Usually Strategies

"I need the house to be under control." "I need you to unload the dishwasher." "I need bedtime to stop taking so long." These sound like needs. And they are, but not the ones you think.

Getting the house under control is one strategy to meet a need for ease, safety, or competence. Having a partner unload the dishwasher is one strategy to meet a need for support or shared responsibility. When we mistake the strategy for the need, we get stuck. There's only one solution available, and it requires someone else to change.

I once picked a fight with my husband because he didn't unload the dishwasher. It wasn't really about the dishwasher. I had needs for support and partnership that I didn't know how to articulate. When I eventually named those — not the strategy, but the actual need — there were suddenly other ways he could have helped me meet them.

The Same Reframe Works for Children

What parents dismiss as children's "wants" works the same way — in reverse.

"They just want attention." "They want to control everything." "They just want to play." These sound like complaints about a child who wants too much. But in almost every case, the want is a need expressing itself the only way a child knows how.

A child who stalls at bedtime is longing for connection — a sense that they matter to you. A child who refuses to brush their teeth is longing for autonomy — to have some say over things that are important to them.

Children don't yet have the language or self-awareness to name what they need. A parent who is longing for rest can say "I need a break" and arrange for one. A two-year-old who is longing for connection can't say "I'm needing more closeness with you right now." What they can do is follow you from room to room until you pay attention to them.

Final Thoughts

When a conflict is framed around a specific strategy, there's usually one solution in mind, and it requires someone else to change. When you can name the underlying need, more solutions appear.

In the next post, we'll look at seven things parents commonly call needs, and what's really underneath each one.
